newsitem.title: CANADA: Peru, Japan leaders discuss hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Japan leaders discuss hostage crisis.

text.p: Leaders of Japan and Peru informally discussed the 45-day-old hostage crisis on Friday and Tokyo stated its concern afterwards that "tensions have been running high" at the rebel-held Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, Japanese sources said.

Fearful of bloodshed in a prolonged standoff, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto began the unscheduled meeting by paying a unscheduled "courtesy visit" to Fujimori at a central Toronto hotel, they said.

Present at the encounter was Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori and a member of a mediation panel seeking to free the 72 rebel-held captives, including about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen, a Japanese government official said.

Following the gathering, a Japanese government source said, "What we are worried about is that communications between the Peruvian government and rebels have broken down and tensions have been running high."
The summit, formally scheduled to begin Saturday, was called three days ago as a rift appeared to widen between Lima and Tokyo on talks with Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
Peru's talks with the guerrillas have been deadlocked for weeks over Lima's refusal to consider the MRTA demand that the government release their 400 jailed comrades.
Tokyo wants Lima to soften its position and allow the rebels' main demand onto the agenda for negotiations, according to a Japanese government source.
Hashimoto told reporters on the plane to Toronto that he would "frankly ask" Fujimori to open negotiations with the MRTA.
The Japanese leader voiced fear the crisis could end in bloodshed if the MRTA harmed the hostages.

Fujimori has said the residence will not be stormed by police unless a hostage is harmed. But he said he was prepared to endure the hostage crisis for months, even raising the specter of the U.S. Embassy crisis in Iran 17 years ago.

"I don't have the faintest idea how long it will be before there is a solution to the crisis. Remember that there was a seizure in Iran that lasted 444 days," Fujimori told Argentina's Clarin newspaper in an interview published after his departure for Canada.
"We are not going to give in to the terrorists' demands. As time goes by, offers made by the government are being progressively reduced," he said.
After the Friday night Fujimori-Hashimoto meeting, a Japanese government source said: "Holding a summit does not necessarily mean that the crisis will be settled soon or the forseeable future."
Among the hostages were Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Cabinet ministers, generals, security chiefs and Bolivia's ambassador to Lima.
Japan's concern deepened this week after provocative action by Peruvian police outside the compound.

Since Jan. 24, police have stepped up the war of nerves, saying they wanted to wear down the rebels' resistance. They sent convoys rumbling past the residence, blasted martial music and buzzed the residence with helicopters and planes.

The Japanese and Peruvian leaders agreed to meet after Hashimoto urged Fujimori to exercise caution to avoid "accidents or incidents" at the diplomatic compound, strewn with rebel mines and booby traps.

The MRTA's international spokesman on Friday warned that Fujimori was playing a dangerous game by suggesting he could wait weeks or even months rather than accept the rebel demands about freeing the jailed guerrillas.
The spokesman, Isaac Velazco, urged Hashimoto to convince Fujimori to seek a political solution to the crisis.
Fujimori and Hashimoto, who met twice in the past four months, chose Canada because they wanted to meet on neutral ground at a convenient mid-point.
Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, was accompanied by two cabinet ministers, five congressmen and his son Kenjy.
